qs.q: What is the primary role of a direct antiglobulin test (DAT) in the workup of an infant with neonatal jaundice?
o: Screening for galactosemia and metabolic blockages
Detecting immune-mediated hemolytic disease via Coombs test
qs.e: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT), also known as the direct Coombs test, helps evaluate for immune-mediated hemolysis in the infant. It is part of the additional laboratory studies.

qs.q: A Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT) is ordered for a newborn presenting with jaundice and suspected haemolytic disease of the newborn. What does a positive DAT indicate?
o: Free antibodies are present in the patient's serum in vitro
Antibodies are already bound to red blood cells in vivo
The patient completely lacks standard ABO and Rh antigens
Sodium metabisulfite has precipitated abnormal haemoglobin
qs.e: The Direct Antiglobulin Test detects antibodies that are already bound to the patient's own red blood cells inside the body. Free serum antibodies are instead detected using the Indirect Antiglobulin Test.

qs.q: A patient experiences an unexpected drop in hemoglobin and mild jaundice approximately 7 days after receiving a blood transfusion. A direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is positive. Which blood group system is most notoriously associated with this type of delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?
qs.e: The Kidd blood group system (Jka, Jkb antigens) is notoriously associated with delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions. Antibodies to Kidd antigens (anti-Jka, anti-Jkb) are often weak or undetectable in pre-transfusion testing but can rapidly increase after re-exposure, leading to extravascular hemolysis typically 3-10 days post-transfusion.

o: The Kidd blood group system, notorious for causing anamnestic antibody responses.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT) detects antibodies or complement on a patient’s red cells, guiding diagnosis of autoimmune hemolytic anemia and transfusion reactions. It informs transfusion safety and treatment choices.

sections.p: DAT identifies IgG or complement bound to red blood cells in vivo. A positive result indicates immune-mediated hemolysis or a transfusion reaction.

t.b: Positive = immune hemolysis or transfusion reaction; negative = unlikely immune cause.

sections.p: DAT itself is not staged, but a positive result prompts evaluation of hemolysis severity via hemoglobin, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, and reticulocyte count.
b: Mild hemolysis: hemoglobin >10 g/dL, mild LDH elevation

sections.p: The most common causes of a positive DAT are warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and transfusion reactions. Other causes include cold agglutinin disease, drug-induced hemolysis, and infections.

t.b: Positive DAT with IgG suggests warm AIHA.
Positive DAT with C3d indicates complement-mediated hemolysis.

sections.p: Patients may have fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine, or splenomegaly. Transfusion reactions present with fever, chills, hypotension, or hemoglobinuria.

t.b: Presence of jaundice or hemoglobinuria supports hemolysis.

sections.p: After a positive DAT, confirm hemolysis and identify the specific antibody. In low-resource settings, a simple antibody screen and crossmatch may suffice.

t.b: Identifies specific antibody for transfusion matching.

sections.p: Severe hemolysis can lead to acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or death. Rapid identification and transfusion avoidance are critical.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute hemolysis with hypotension or renal failure
Severe anemia with rapid drop in hemoglobin

faq.q: What does a positive DAT mean?
faq.a: It shows antibodies or complement attached to red cells, indicating immune hemolysis or a transfusion reaction.

faq.q: Can DAT be negative in hemolytic anemia?
faq.a: Yes, if hemolysis is non-immune or antibodies are below detection limits.

faq.q: Do I need a blood transfusion if DAT is positive?
faq.a: Only if the patient is symptomatic or severely anemic; otherwise treat the underlying cause.
